messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla, a 52-year-old project manager known for her calm authority and meticulous planning, had always navigated the complexities of her high-rise office with a steady hand. That was before the attack. She and her husband had been at an outdoor food festival downtown, a rare weekend indulgence, when the first explosion tore through the crowd. The initial disbelief gave way to a primal terror as chaos erupted. In the ensuing moments, she witnessed acts of violence she couldn't process, the screams of the injured punctuated by the blare of approaching sirens. Layla remembers being separated from her husband, the frantic search through the panicked crowd, and then the overwhelming sound of helicopters, their blades beating the air above as police swarmed the area. She found her husband an hour later, physically unharmed but both irrevocably altered.

In the six months since, Layla has found that the city she once commanded from her corner office has become a landscape of threats. The triggers are mundane, yet potent. A police car, lights flashing as it pulls over a speeding driver on her commute, is no longer a symbol of order. For Layla, the sight sends a jolt of adrenaline through her body, and a conviction immediately follows: she is exposed. She becomes certain that every other driver, every pedestrian on the sidewalk, can see her terror, that the memory of what she endured is somehow written on her face for the world to read. This feeling of being transparently vulnerable reinforces a deeper, more painful belief that she has lost the competent, self-assured person she once was.

This erosion of her identity is most acute at work, the one place she used to feel most herself. Last week, the percussive thrum of a news helicopter passing her office window sent her diving for cover under her desk, a reflexive act that left her trembling and ashamed. As her team members stared in confused silence, she felt a profound sense of alienation from her own life. She had come to believe that the happy, capable woman who used to lead these people was gone forever, replaced by this frightened, fragile stranger. She now looks at old photographs and feels a sense of mourning for the smiling woman in them, convinced that her own capacity for joy and ease has been permanently extinguished.

The world now seems to conspire to remind her of her brokenness. Seeing a heated argument on the street or catching a violent scene on the news in the office breakroom brings back the festival with a visceral rush. Each time, it’s not just fear she feels, but a confirmation of her new reality. She believes that she is no longer the person who could navigate the world with confidence. That Layla is gone, and this new, perpetually miserable version is all that remains. Her husband’s attempts to comfort her feel hollow, as if he’s speaking to a ghost of the woman he married. She has started avoiding client meetings and delegating tasks that require her to be in public, a shift that hasn't gone unnoticed by her superiors. It was after receiving a gentle inquiry from her director about her recent performance that Layla finally made an appointment. She came to therapy not with a hope of being cured, but with a quiet, desperate plea to find out if there was any part of her old self left to salvage.
